Accompanimental Textures: Practice for Chapter 14

Hear and try the accompaniment patterns of Chapter 14 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom on the site’s backing band: chorale texture, arpeggios and Alberti bass, block chords in the 1 (2) & and Barbara Ann rhythms, repeated chords, afterbeats and off-beats, the 3–2 son clave and 3+3+2, and riff bass lines, with a listening quiz and the book’s examples.

This page goes with Chapter 14, Accompanimental Textures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. The book shows each texture in notation and in recordings. Here you can play each one: the site’s backing band plays the same chords in each texture, and you switch between textures while it plays.

How the demos work: press ▶ Play, then try the buttons under it. The band keeps going and changes texture at the next bar. Who plays turns each part on and off. Under the buttons the band’s whole pass is written out when Play starts, before it sounds, so you can see what is coming. (The quiz shows the notes only once you have answered.) Tempo and Stop are in the strip at the bottom of the page. The quiz at the end plays a texture without naming it, and you say which one it is.

14.1 Texture

The book looks at texture two ways. Vertically: how many notes sound at once (how full the chords are, how many voices there are). Horizontally: how busy the rhythm is (are the most common note values long or short?). Read 14.1

Below are the same four chords played three ways. Held chords are full but slow. Repeated eighth notes keep the same notes and make the rhythm busy. An arpeggio is busy too, but it plays one note at a time, so it is thinner at any one moment.

NoteListen: the book’s two examples

14.2 Chorale texture

In a chorale texture there is a new chord for (nearly) every melody note, so all the parts move in the same rhythm. This is also called homorhythmic. A hymn played on the piano is the plainest case. The band’s hymn style below holds each chord until the next one, with three voices over the bass. With a melody on top, it would be a chorale texture. Read 14.2 · Pattern lesson: Hymn, four parts

The second button is the book’s quarter-note texture: a chord on every beat. The book’s practice exercises ask for it (17.7, exercise 3).

NoteListen: the book’s chorale examples

14.3 Arpeggiated accompaniments

An arpeggio plays a chord’s notes one after another instead of all together. The bass usually holds the root underneath, as in the book’s first example, Beethoven’s Moonlight Sonata. The band can arpeggiate up and back down, or rock between the lowest and highest notes. Alberti bass goes low, high, middle, high, again and again. Read 14.3 · Pattern lessons: Arpeggio, up and down · Arpeggio, low and high · Alberti bass

The book points out the Alberti pattern in a Mozart sonata, and the same pattern lower down and in E minor in “Pipeline”. Here is Alberti bass on its own, in major (bass off: the pattern supplies its own low note):

NoteListen: the book’s arpeggio examples

14.4 Block chord accompaniments

Block chords strike all the notes of the chord together. What makes one block-chord accompaniment different from another is its rhythm. The book names four:

  • “1 (2) &”: two chords a bar, on beat 1 and on the and of 2. Count it aloud and stay silent on the number in brackets.
  • The “Barbara Ann” rhythm, over two bars: 1 2 3 (4) & | (1) & (2) & 3.
  • Repeated eighth-note chords: a chord on every eighth note, in classical music and in rock.
  • Repeated quarter-note chords: a chord on every beat.

Read 14.4 · Pattern lessons: Charleston (the 1 (2) & rhythm) · Barbara Ann · Driving eighths · Quarter-note chords

The band calls the “1 (2) &” rhythm the Charleston: jazz musicians use that name for the same two hits. The book points out that the bass in “Let’s Get It On” and “Thinking Out Loud” has a similar rhythm. The bass here plays the dotted 1, and of 2, 3 line with it. Turn the drums and bass off to hear the chords alone.

NoteListen: “1 (2) &” and Barbara Ann
NoteListen: repeated eighths and quarters

14.5 Afterbeats and off-beats

Afterbeats is Arnold Schoenberg’s word for repeated chords that come after the downbeat. Off-beats are chords that keep to the upbeats and stay off the downbeats. The book looks at two styles built on off-beats: polka and reggae. Read 14.5 · Pattern lessons: Boom-chick · Every off-beat

Polka: the bass on the beat and the chord in between. The band counts the bar in four, so the chords fall on 2 and 4. Counted in a fast two, those are the off-beats.

Reggae: short chords on the and of every beat, often on electric guitar, over a drum part (the one-drop) that leaves beat 1 empty.

NoteListen: the book’s afterbeat, polka and reggae examples

14.6 The 3–2 son clave and 3+3+2

The 3–2 son clave is a two-bar rhythm at the root of Afro-Cuban music: three strokes in the first bar and two in the second. Its first bar divides eight eighth notes into 3+3+2. In popular music it is also called the Bo Diddley beat. The 3+3+2 bar on its own is everywhere in pop. In sixteenth notes it is called tresillo, and the book follows it into the habanera and the reggaeton beat. Read 14.6 · Pattern lessons: 3–2 clave in the chords · 3+3+2 · The Bo Diddley beat on drums · Dembow (reggaeton)

The habanera bass (Bizet, Carmen) and the reggaeton beat: long chords, the bass on 3+3+2, the dembow on the drums.

NoteListen: clave and 3+3+2, from the book’s list

The book’s section has more than thirty examples. The full list, with notation of each rhythm, is in 14.6.

14.7 Distinctive bass lines

Some songs are known by their riff: a short bass (or guitar) figure repeated under the chords. The band’s bass lines are not those riffs. They are general patterns that fit any chords. But they show how much of a style’s character comes from a repeating bass figure. Drums and bass only: Read 14.7

NoteFor teachers
  • The band: the demos run on the site’s Backing Track band. Each button changes one band setting (comping rhythm, bass line or drum groove) and the change takes effect at the next bar. The same patterns, each with a step-by-step lesson, are on the Pattern lessons pages.
  • Names: the band’s names for some rhythms differ from the book’s. The book’s “1 (2) &” is the band’s Charleston, its afterbeats in polka are the band’s boom-chick, and its reggae off-beats are the band’s every off-beat. The quiz uses the book’s names.
  • Not here: the band does not play the book’s specific songs or riffs (14.7), afterbeats as passing figures in thirds (the Mozart example in 14.5), or 3+3+2 in sixteenth notes against a slow beat. The book’s listening lists are much longer than the selections here.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube. “Pretty Thing” (14.6) is no longer available there, so it is left out.
  • Not checked by ear: the patterns were checked in notation and by the band’s tests. Whether each one sounds like the book’s examples has not been checked by listening.
